name: Vitamin K eye cream

lead: Vitamin K eye cream is applied under the eyes and marketed for dark circles with a vascular or bruise-like look, with the aim of a lighter, brighter under-eye. Vitamin K is a fat-soluble vitamin known for its role in blood clotting.

Proponents link that clotting role to reducing blood pooling beneath thin skin. No clinical studies of topical vitamin K for dark circles were found. Dark circles have many causes, including anatomy, pigmentation, allergies, eye rubbing, medications and thin skin.

paras: It is used as an ordinary cosmetic cream, applied under the eyes as part of a skincare routine, often alongside sunscreen and other eye-area products.

Reference material notes no known toxicity from high oral intakes of K1 or K2, while intravenous injection can cause severe reactions; those findings concern oral and injected forms, not creams. As with any product near the eyes, irritation is possible.

angle.text: Vitamin K eye cream is marketed to fade the bluish look of under-eye circles that have a visible-vessel component, for a brighter under-eye. The sources reviewed contain no clinical studies of it for this use.

lead: Vitamin K eye cream is a topical cosmetic product containing vitamin K, applied under the eyes and marketed for dark circles that are thought to have a vascular component, meaning visible blood vessels or pooled blood beneath thin skin.

Vitamin K is a group of fat-soluble vitamins: K1 (phylloquinone) from plants and K2 (menaquinones) from animal and fermented foods, with a role as a cofactor for the carboxylation of clotting factors [1].

Periorbital dark circles are attributed to several causes including anatomy, allergies and eye rubbing, medications, thin skin and increased pigmentation [2]. No clinical studies of topical vitamin K for this condition were found in the sources reviewed.
infobox: Dark circles with a vascular component

paras: Reference text on periorbital dark circles lists multiple possible contributors, including bone structure, thin lower-eyelid skin that makes underlying vessels visible, allergic congestion, melanin excess, sleep loss and ageing changes [2]. Treatments named there include vitamin C, caffeine, hydroquinone, lasers, fillers and fat grafting; vitamin K cream is not mentioned in that article [2].

Vitamin K works as a cofactor for gamma-glutamyl carboxylase, which modifies clotting factors so that they can bind calcium [1]. That clotting role is the basis on which the topical product is marketed for bruise-like discoloration, though the reference articles consulted do not address topical use for dark circles [2][1].

Reference text notes that no toxicity is linked to high oral doses of vitamins K1 and K2, and that intravenous K1 can cause severe reactions in rare cases [1]. People taking warfarin are advised to keep vitamin K intake consistent [1]. These statements concern oral and injected vitamin K and have not been shown to apply to creams.
